title: Kicker Candle
teaches: The Kicker as we trade it: a leader already set up, a real red day that closes weak at support, then a day that gaps up at least 1.5%, trades through the red day's high and never fills the gap; the buy is a market order over the red high on the Kicker day (never the close), the stop a few cents under the Kicker day's low or 3.5% under the entry if closer, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, and a stop-out is the plan working.

walkthroughs.title: BBY, July 2013: the cleanest two candles on a base
steps: BBY, late June 2013. A leader coiled in a tight 6.2% range. Then a red day, down 1.8%, closing on its low.
Looks like a breakdown, so sellers bail. Next morning, July 1, it gaps up 2.1% over that close and the gap holds.
It trades through the red day's high: buy at market, 27.97. Stop 27.67, a few cents under the low. That's 1.1%.
If the gap fills, it's wrong. Instead it closes up 8.8%, near the high. 3R came in one day.

walkthroughs.title: COHR, January 2024: a fill at the open
steps: COHR spent six weeks on a shelf, riding its rising short-term averages. Then a red day, down 1.8%, closing near the low.
January 16, 2024, it gaps up 2.6% and opens just over the red high. Your market order fills at the open, 42.83.
There's no low yet, so start the stop 3.5% under, 41.33. At 10:00, raise it to the 30-minute low if that's higher.
The gap never fills. It closes up 8.2% and hits 3R on day 4. First sell is your call, into a push.

walkthroughs.title: ATRO, June 2026: the trims and the trail
steps: A red day drops ATRO 2.7% to just under its 20 EMA, June 2026. It closes near the low.
June 11 it gaps up 3.0% and trades through the red high. Buy at market, 68.80. Stop 67.36, 2.1% away.
Closes on the high, up 15.1%. 3R on day 1 is too soon to sell. Breakeven on the stop is your call.
It ran 13.8R in two weeks, then gave most of it back. Sell into the push, or you hand it back.

questions.q: A leader has based quietly for weeks. Which two candles turn that base into a Kicker?
choices: Weak red day, then a gap up
Green day, then red under its low
A doji, then a small inside day
Two red days that each gap lower
questions.answer: Weak red day, then a gap up
questions.why: A weak red day, then a gap up. The red day is a real drop that closes near its low, right at support. It looks like a breakdown, so people sell it. The next morning it gaps up, trades through the red day's high and never comes back to the red close. Everyone who sold yesterday is now trapped. A baby red candle or a doji doesn't count. Nobody got scared on those.
questions.lesson_line: A red day that looks like a breakdown, then a gap up. That's the trap.

wrong.Green day, then red under its low: That's a stock breaking down after strength. A Kicker goes the other way: red first, then the gap up.
wrong.A doji, then a small inside day: Nobody's scared on a doji, and an inside day has no gap. No trap, no kick.
wrong.Two red days that each gap lower: That's sellers winning two days running. The Kicker day gaps up.

questions.simple: A real red day that closes weak at support, then a gap up that traps the people who sold.

reasons: names the proposed 1.5% gap line
rests on the house card plus one public UCT definition

questions.q: A leader prints a tiny red candle, a near doji. The next morning it gaps up 2.2% through that high. That's a Kicker.
questions.why: False. That's a breakout, not a Kicker. GWW did exactly this: a red body of 0.04% of price and a drop of 0.4%, then a 2.2% gap. Looks great. But the whole point of the red day is to scare people out at support. A doji scares nobody, so nobody's trapped when it gaps. Judge it as a regular breakout instead.
questions.lesson_line: No trapped sellers, no kick. After a doji it's just a breakout.
questions.simple: False. A doji scares nobody out, so there's no one trapped and no kick.

reasons: settled card criterion, two agreeing house facts

questions.q: You want the Kicker tomorrow. Where does your buy go?
choices: A cent over the red day's high
The Kicker close, at market
A cent under the red day's low
A cent over the red day's open
questions.answer: A cent over the red day's high
questions.why: One cent over 11.04, the red day's high, on the Kicker day only. It's a market order that fires as price trades through. JBI filled right there, at 11.05. Once price is over the red high, everyone who sold the red day is underwater. Wait for the close and you just pay more, with your stop further away. Mark 11.04 the night before and set an alert.
questions.lesson_line: The trade through the red high is your buy. The close is too late.

wrong.The Kicker close, at market: Buying the close means paying up after the move. The buy is the trade through the red high.
wrong.A cent under the red day's low: That's buying weakness. We buy strength, over the red high.
wrong.A cent over the red day's open: The open isn't the line that traps anyone. The red high is.

questions.simple: A cent over 11.04, the red day's high, as price trades through it. Never at the close.

questions.why: True. In Red we're mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. A Kicker is a bet that yesterday's sellers got it wrong. In a falling market they're often right. A bounce in a Red market looks like a Kicker and isn't. LLY in March 2020 looked perfect and was stopped out the next session. I want Green or Yellow for these, and Orange only for an A+.
questions.lesson_line: Check the market first. In Red, the Kicker waits.
questions.simple: True. In a Red market we stay mostly in cash, because bounces there fail.

questions.q: People say the gap held today. What has to be true for that?
choices: It stays over the red close
It closes above its open
It opens over the red day's high
It holds above the 50-day
questions.answer: It stays over the red close
questions.why: It stayed over the red day's close all day. That's the test. On JBI the Kicker day's low never got back to the red close. If price trades back down to that close, the gap has filled. Yesterday's sellers got out at their price, so nobody's trapped anymore. That's when I lose interest. Where it opened against the red high doesn't matter for this.
questions.lesson_line: Hold above the red close, or the trap is off.

wrong.It closes above its open: That's about the candle's color. A gap can hold on a day that fades from its open.
wrong.It opens over the red day's high: That's where it opened. Holding means it never came back to the red close.
wrong.It holds above the 50-day: The 50-day is the bigger picture. The gap holds against the red close.

questions.simple: The gap held if price never traded back down to the red day's close.

reasons: gap-holds is a proposed card criterion

questions.q: Before you plan a Kicker, what do you want to see behind the red day?
choices: On a base or an orderly pullback
After a vertical run with no base
Under a falling 200-day
On any earnings gap
questions.answer: On a base or an orderly pullback
questions.why: A base or an orderly pullback. A Kicker works on a leader that's already set up. Tight closes before the red day, above the 200-day, with the 50-day flat or rising. SWKS sat on a flat six-week base over a rising 50-day. That's the spot. It's a bit stretched off that 50-day, and the 200-day is way down there, so this is a later base in a long run. Still a base. The base is where buyers showed they want the stock. The Kicker tells you they're back.
questions.lesson_line: No base, no setup. The Kicker sits on a leader that's already resting.

wrong.After a vertical run with no base: That's a stock mid-run. No base means nothing tight to put a stop under.
wrong.Under a falling 200-day: We don't buy stocks under the 200-day. That's a hard no.
wrong.On any earnings gap: The first session after a report is an earnings gapper. We grade that as its own setup, a Power Earnings Gap.

questions.simple: A leader that's already set up, resting in a base or an orderly pullback.

deeper.trap: On 2011-08-03 IDCC looked like a Kicker: red day -5.8%, gap 5.7%, +13.8% on 2.7x. But the prior 20 closes spanned 44.1% after a 60% burst, so there was no base. It was taken anyway and stopped the next session at 0.0R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-025, the earnings-day Kicker)

questions.story: Here's the red day of a Kicker. Look at the weeks behind it.

questions.q: In the candle books, the bullish kicker is a black candle, a gap up, then a white candle, both with no wicks.
questions.why: True. That's the strict textbook version. Both candles are full bodies, with no wicks at either end, and a gap between them. Ours is looser. I want a real red day that closes weak at support. Then a gap up that trades through the red high and never fills. Where it happens matters more to me than a perfect shape.
questions.lesson_line: The books want a perfect shape. We want the right spot.
questions.simple: True. The textbook kicker is two candles with no wicks and a gap between them.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski describes a tall black marubozu, an upward gap, then a tall white marubozu. Schwab says neither candle has shadows. Ours is looser. We want a real red day closing weak near its low at support. Then a gap up that trades through the red high and never fills.

reasons: two Tier 2 publishers agree; both quotes re-opened and found on their pages 2026-11-11

questions.q: You're planning a Kicker. How far under your entry can the stop sit before it's no longer a clean Kicker?
choices: 3.5% under your entry
3% under your entry
5.5% under your entry
Under the base low
questions.why: 3.5%. The stop goes a few cents under the Kicker day's low, the low of the day. If 3.5% under your entry is closer, that's your stop instead. So 3.5% is the most a Kicker gets. It's tight for a reason. A real Kicker shouldn't come back much. If it does, the trap didn't work and I want out small. If the honest stop has to be wider, I pass.
questions.lesson_line: A Kicker gets 3.5% at most. Wider than that, pass.

wrong.3% under your entry: About 3% is our normal feel for a stop. The Kicker gets its own 3.5%.
wrong.5.5% under your entry: Too wide. If the stop has to sit that far away, it isn't a clean Kicker.
wrong.Under the base low: The base low can be miles away. The stop sits under the Kicker day itself.

questions.simple: 3.5%. A real Kicker shouldn't need more room, so a wider stop means pass.

reasons: rests on the owner's Kicker stop ruling (3.5% cap)

questions.q: Most real Kickers have no earnings report behind the gap.
questions.why: True. A Kicker is short-term positioning. There's no report behind it. The stock shook people out on the red day and snapped right back. When the gap day is the first session after a report, it's a different trade. We call that an earnings gapper and grade it as a PEG, a Power Earnings Gap. So check the earnings date before you call anything a Kicker.
questions.lesson_line: Kickers are positioning. The day after a report belongs to earnings.
questions.simple: True. A Kicker is positioning, and a gap the day after a report is an earnings gapper.

deeper.counter: LUV on 2026-01-29 passed every shape test: a weak red day, a gap and a strong close out of a base. But the gap day was the earnings reaction day, after a report on 2026-01-28. So we graded it as a Power Earnings Gap, not a Kicker.

reasons: rests on a held decision (D-025, the earnings-day Kicker)

questions.sentence: A base or an orderly pullback: the last 20 closes span ___% or less of price.
questions.why: 15%. A base or an orderly pullback means the last 20 closes span 15% or less of price. A wider span is not a base.
questions.lesson_line: Twenty closes inside a 15% span: that is the base.
questions.simple: The last 20 closes must span 15% or less of price, which marks a tight base.

deeper.trap: The span is a share of price, not dollars. A stock mid-run that spans far more than 15% is not a base, however tidy the last candle looks.

reasons: the 15% span is a proposed criterion value that may change

questions.q: A leader's base just printed a red day. Where do you want it to close for a Kicker tomorrow?
choices: At support, like the 20 EMA
At a fresh 52-week high
In free fall, far from averages
Near its high, after a dip
questions.why: Right at support, like the 20 EMA or the 50-day, or down at the last week's lows. And near the low of its own range. That's what makes it look like a breakdown. People sell the break into the line. Then the gap up traps every one of them. A red day in free fall, or one closing near its high, doesn't set that trap.
questions.lesson_line: The red day falls into a line and closes weak. That's the trap.

wrong.At a fresh 52-week high: That's a breakout, not a breakdown. Nobody sold a break, so nobody's trapped.
wrong.In free fall, far from averages: That's a shock day, not an orderly pullback into a line. It looks like a Kicker and isn't.
wrong.Near its high, after a dip: A close near the high scares nobody. The red day closes weak, near its low.

questions.simple: At support and near its low, so it looks like a breakdown and traps the sellers.

reasons: the support thresholds are card numbers that may change
fixed before

questions.q: You own a Kicker. Day 2 prints a big bearish engulfing candle, but your stop isn't hit. That candle alone isn't a reason to sell.
questions.why: True. The stop is your exit. A bearish engulfing candle is a red body that swallows the day before. It looks scary. But if price is still over your stop, the trade hasn't failed. When I meddle with positions on a candle, I mostly make the wrong call. Stick to the stop. If the trade's really failing, it takes you out at the loss you planned.
questions.lesson_line: A candle isn't an exit. The stop is.
questions.simple: True. Only the stop ends a failed trade, so a scary candle alone isn't a sell.

deeper.example: PGR, bought 2023-03-16. On day 2 it closed back under the red high, and the stop traded the same day. The stop did the work, not the candle.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)

questions.q: The app flags a Kicker on a $6 stock that trades $3 million a day. What does a stock need before we'd even look?
choices: $10 and $20 million a day
$15 and $50 million a day
$2 and $10,000 a day
Nothing if it's a real leader
questions.why: At least $10 a share and $20 million traded a day. This one fails both. Here's why it matters. You have to get out at your stop. In a thin stock your stop can fill well under where you set it. The app's detector looks much lower, down to $2 and $10,000 a day. So an alert tells you nothing about liquidity. Check it yourself.
questions.lesson_line: Ten dollars a share, twenty million a day. Below that, we don't look.

wrong.$15 and $50 million a day: Too high. Our floor is $10 a share and $20 million a day.
wrong.$2 and $10,000 a day: That's the app detector's floor, far under ours. It fires on stocks we'd never trade.
wrong.Nothing if it's a real leader: Every stock has to clear the floor. We don't even watch thin names.

questions.simple: $10 a share and $20 million a day, so you can get out at your stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is the app's alert. The detector's floor is $2 and $10,000 a day, so it can fire on a stock we would never watch. Check our own $10 and $20 million floor before you plan the buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: The honest Kicker stop is 3.5% under your entry, too wide for your risk budget. You tighten it to 2% so the size fits.
questions.why: False. The stop comes from the chart. It's a few cents under the low of the day, or 3.5% under your entry if that's closer. The size comes from the stop, never the other way around. A 2% stop here sits inside the normal noise. You'd get shaken out of a trade that was working. If 3.5% doesn't fit your risk, skip it. There's always another setup.
questions.lesson_line: Never fit the stop to the size. Fit the size to the stop, or skip.
questions.simple: False. You size to the stop, and if the honest stop doesn't fit, you skip it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5)

questions.q: When are you looking at your first sell?
choices: Day 3 at the earliest
Day 1, the buy day
Day 2, the next morning
Only at the time stop on day 10
questions.why: Day 3 at the earliest. I very rarely sell on day 1, even after a fast 3R like AXON's. A Kicker that strong is the kind you want to give room. Sell on day 1 and you cut your best trades short. I look to sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Which one is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: We rarely sell on day 1. The first sell waits for the push.

wrong.Day 1, the buy day: We very rarely sell on day 1. A fast start is a reason to give it room.
wrong.Day 2, the next morning: Still too early. We wait for day 3 at the earliest.
wrong.Only at the time stop on day 10: The time stop is for slow trades. A working trade gets its first sell into a push.

questions.simple: Day 3 at the earliest. Strong trades need room, so we rarely sell on day one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51: a third at 3R is the hard rule)

questions.story: You bought the Kicker day at 21.44, stop 20.70. It hits 3R within a day.

questions.q: A stock trades 400,000 shares a day. Your Kicker size comes to 20,000 shares. That size is fine.
questions.why: False. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. 20,000 shares is five times that here. Why it matters: on the day you need out, you'd be a big chunk of the selling. Your own order pushes the price down and your stop fills worse. Cut the size to 1% of the volume, or trade a more liquid stock.
questions.lesson_line: Size to the stock too. One percent of its daily volume is the ceiling.
questions.simple: False. We never own more than 1% of the daily volume, so we can get out clean.

reasons: one cited fact only
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: You want your 3R level marked before tomorrow's open. Where is it?
questions.why: 132.83. One R is what you risk a share: 122.84 minus 119.51 is 3.33. Put three of those on top of your 122.84 fill and you're at 132.83. Mark it the night you buy. R puts every trade on the same ruler. But 3R isn't a sell order. AMD got there within two days, and the first sell was still a judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. It's a ruler, not a sell order.
questions.simple: Take your fill minus your stop, times three, and add it to the fill.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (a third off at 3R)

wrong.$126.17: That's only one R on top of the fill. You need three.
wrong.$129.50: You added three R to the stop. Start from your fill.
wrong.$112.85: You took three R off the fill. 3R is above your buy.

questions.q: Four leaders each print a red day right at the 20 EMA. Which one sets up the best Kicker for tomorrow?
choices: Closes near its low, at the 20 EMA
Closes mid-range, at the 20 EMA
Closes near its high, at the 20 EMA
Closes near its open, a tiny body
questions.answer: Closes near its low, at the 20 EMA
questions.why: The one closing near its low. That's the real drop, the one that looks like a breakdown. People sell it. When it gaps up through that high tomorrow, they're trapped. A mid-range close doesn't scare anybody, so the gap after it is just a gap up. ISRG is our example of that. BBY is the good one: down 1.8%, closing at 2% of its range, right into support.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close at support sets the trap. A mid-range close is just a gap up.

wrong.Closes near its open, a tiny body: That's a baby candle. Nobody's scared, so nobody's trapped.
wrong.Closes mid-range, at the 20 EMA: A mid-range close doesn't look like a breakdown. ISRG did this and it was just a regular gap up.
wrong.Closes near its high, at the 20 EMA: Closing near the high is buyers winning the day. Nobody sold a break.

questions.simple: The one that closes near its low, because that's the one that scares sellers out.

deeper.example: BBY, 2013: a 6.2% tight range into support. The red day fell 1.8% and closed at 2% of its range. Next morning it gapped up 2.1% and the gap held, and it closed up 8.8%.

questions.q: The Kicker day opens wild over the red high and you'd rather not buy the open. A cent over the first 30-minute high is a fair way in.
questions.why: True. That's our second entry, the opening-range break. Mark the high of the first 30-minute bar, 9:30 to 10:00, and buy a cent over it. It's handy when the open is wild and you'd rather let the first half hour settle. Your stop goes a few cents under that bar's low, or 3.5% under the entry if that's closer. Pick one entry, one price, one stop. We buy once.
questions.lesson_line: Two ways in: over the red high, or over the first 30-minute high.
questions.simple: True. You can buy a cent over the high of the first half hour instead of the open.

questions.q: The red day closed at 44.10. The Kicker day opens at 44.75. What is the gap, as a percent of the red close, to two decimals?

questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap. A gap a hair short of the line is not a gap.
questions.simple: The gap is 1.47%, which is under the 1.5% line, so this is not a Kicker gap.

Take the one closer to your entry, 27.00. The low of the day sits more than 3.5% away here. So the cap does the work and keeps the loss to what a Kicker should cost.
questions.lesson_line: Two stops, one answer: take the one closer to your entry.
questions.simple: The cap is closer than the low here, so it sets your stop.

deeper.trap: Anchoring on the low. A few cents under 26.90 feels safe. But it sits further from the 27.98 fill than 3.5% does, so it risks more than the cap allows. The stop closer to your entry wins.

rests on the owner's rulebook (Kicker stop ruling, F62)

Your stop stays where it was, so every cent you pay up widens it and shrinks your shares. If it had opened past 4%, wait for a morning flush that curls back up.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the open against your buy point. Past 4%, you're chasing.
questions.simple: It's 3.4% past the buy point, inside our 4% line, so you can still buy it.

the 4% chase limit is the owner's rulebook (C28); the flush way in is the owner's ruling D-022

questions.q: Which of these ends the trade before you buy?
choices: It trades back to the red close
It gaps up 2.4% on heavy volume
It trades over the red day's high
It opens under the red day's high
questions.answer: It trades back to the red close
questions.why: It trades back to the red day's close. That fills the gap before the trigger, so there is no trade. The Kicker also needs a trade over the red day's high, which is the trigger itself. A gap of 1.5% or more is what you want, and a filled gap is what kills the setup.
questions.lesson_line: A filled gap is a dead Kicker. Walk away.

wrong.It gaps up 2.4% on heavy volume: A gap of 1.5% or more is what you want. A filled gap is what kills it.
wrong.It opens under the red day's high: Opening under the red high does not end it. The buy-stop one cent over the red high simply waits until the stock trades through.

questions.simple: If the stock trades back down to the red day's close, the gap has filled and there is no trade.

reasons: inverse-gap criterion is a proposed card rule

questions.q: Tomorrow's Kicker looks clean. Do you plan the buy?
choices: No, a report is inside 3 sessions
Yes, it is a Kicker, not earnings
No, it is really an earnings gapper
Yes, then sell before the report
questions.story: The red day. Tomorrow it trades through this high, a clean Kicker. The company reports after tomorrow's close.
questions.answer: No, a report is inside 3 sessions
questions.why: No. We don't buy anything new in the 3 sessions before a report, and this one reports right after the Kicker day. A clean chart doesn't change that. The report can gap it straight through your stop, and no stop protects you from that. GOOGL did exactly that in 2020: Kicker, report that night, gap down to 0R. Check the earnings date before you plan any buy.
questions.lesson_line: No new buys in the 3 sessions before a report.

wrong.Yes, it is a Kicker, not earnings: The report window still applies. A clean Kicker doesn't get a pass.
wrong.Yes, then sell before the report: That's still a new buy inside the window. We just don't take it.
wrong.No, it is really an earnings gapper: An earnings gapper is the session after a report. This report hasn't come out yet.

questions.simple: No. A report is coming right after the Kicker day, and a report gap skips your stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is a clean Kicker. It can look perfect and still sit inside the window. GOOGL on 2020-02-03 reported after the Kicker's own close and gapped down the next morning. AVGO on 2024-03-07 did the same. Check the calendar before the buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, the 3-day earnings window)

questions.q: It's 10:00. What do you do with your stop?
choices: Raise it under 41.30
Leave it at 40.53
Move it to breakeven, 42.00
Lower it for more room
questions.story: You were filled at the open at 42.00 with the stop at 40.53. It is 10:00 and the first 30-minute low is 41.30.
questions.why: Raise it to a few cents under 41.30. Your open fill started with the 3.5% stop at 40.53, because there was no low yet. Now there is one. The first 30-minute low is 41.30, higher than 40.53, so the stop comes up. That's less risk on the same trade. A stop only moves up, never down. Breakeven comes later, between 2R and 5R or at your first sell.
questions.lesson_line: On an open fill, the stop comes up to the 30-minute low at 10:00.

wrong.Leave it at 40.53: That was only there because the day had no low yet. Now it does, and it's higher.
wrong.Move it to breakeven, 42.00: Too soon. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell.

questions.simple: Raise it to just under the first half-hour low, since that's higher than 40.53.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (a stop only moves up, A4) and the Kicker open-fill rule
fixed before (variety rewrite)

questions.q: Close is near. What do you do with the position?
choices: Hold, and leave the stop in place
Sell it all at the close, it failed
Move the stop up to breakeven now
Add on the dip to lower the cost
questions.story: You bought the Kicker over the red high. At the close it sits back under that high. It never traded back to the red close and is above your stop.
questions.answer: Hold, and leave the stop in place
questions.why: Hold, and leave the stop where it is. A close back under the red high says the trap didn't fully hold. That's a warning, and it lowers the grade. It's not an exit. Your stop is the line where the trade is wrong, and price is still above it. Sell on the candle and you're guessing. Let the stop decide.
questions.lesson_line: A weak close is a warning. Only the stop sells you.

wrong.Sell it all at the close, it failed: It hasn't failed. It's still over your stop. The weak close is a warning.
wrong.Move the stop up to breakeven now: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at your first sell. Not on a weak close.
wrong.Add on the dip to lower the cost: We buy once, at one price. A dip isn't a second entry.

questions.simple: Hold. A weak close is a warning, but only the stop sells you.

reasons: rests on the owner's settled no-early-exit ruling (D-136)

questions.q: It gapped under your stop. Where's your stop now?
choices: 98.20, the first 30-minute low
100.00, the stop as it was
Out at once, the loss is past 2R
The open, 98.50, the gap price
questions.story: You bought at 103.50 with the stop at 100.00. The next morning it gaps open at 98.50. The first 30-minute low is 98.20.
questions.why: 98.20, the low of the first 30-minute bar. A gap through your stop is the one time a stop moves. The open isn't the decision, it's just the first print. So you let the first 30 minutes play out and use that bar's low as the new stop. Here 98.20 is still inside a 2R loss, so you stay in. If those 30 minutes had taken you past 2R, you'd get out.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop: the first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Out at once, the loss is past 2R: It isn't. At 98.20 the loss is still inside 2R.
wrong.The open, 98.50, the gap price: The open is just the first print. The first 30-minute low is the stop.
wrong.100.00, the stop as it was: Price is already under it. The first 30-minute low takes over.

questions.simple: The first half-hour low, 98.20, because the first 30 minutes decide a gap through the stop.

deeper.trap: Treating the open as your stop. 98.50 is only the first print. Wait out the first 30 minutes and use that bar's low. Get out only if that loss runs past 2R.

reasons: a computed key (the loss at the low against the 2R ceiling)
rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, the gap rule)

questions.q: It's almost the close and you missed the trigger. Do you buy it now?
choices: No, the trigger's gone
Yes, a strong close confirms
No, buy tomorrow's open
Yes, with the 3.5% stop
questions.story: The Kicker day ran through the red high and closed strong, near its high. You were away from the screen.
questions.why: No. The buy was the trade through the red high, and you missed it. That happens. Buy the close and you pay the top of the day, with your stop way down under the low. Same risk budget, fewer shares, worse spot. A strong close is how we grade the chart afterward. It's not a buy signal. Put it on your list and wait for the next real setup.
questions.lesson_line: Missed the trigger, let it go. Don't buy the close.

wrong.Yes, a strong close confirms: A strong close grades the chart afterward. It isn't a buy.
wrong.No, buy tomorrow's open: The red-high trigger is a Kicker-day trigger only. Tomorrow needs a new setup.
wrong.Yes, with the 3.5% stop: The stop doesn't fix a late entry. We don't buy the close.

questions.simple: No. The trigger was earlier in the day, and buying the close means paying the top.

reasons: a missed-day second chance is a held decision (D-026), so no late entry is taught

questions.q: Your Kicker would fill at 55.00. The 9 EMA sits at 49.00. How far over the 9 EMA is that?
questions.why: 12.2%, so you pass. 55.00 minus 49.00 is 6.00. Divide 6.00 by the 9 EMA, 49.00, and you get 12.2%. We skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA. Stocks that stretched tend to snap back to the line. Buy up here and a normal pullback is a loss, or your stop has to be huge. Divide by the 9 EMA, not your fill.
questions.lesson_line: More than 10% over the 9 EMA is too stretched to buy.
questions.simple: It's 12.2% over the 9 EMA, past our 10% line, so it's too stretched to buy.

deeper.counter: Two tests can disagree. The 4% chase limit measures the fill against the buy point. The 10% stretch test measures the fill against the 9 EMA. A buy can pass one and fail the other, and it must pass both.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)

wrong.112.2%: You divided the fill by the 9 EMA and forgot to take off the one.
wrong.89.1%: That's upside down. Divide the gap by the 9 EMA.

questions.q: Yesterday, the red day, closed at 49.80 near its low. Its high was 51.50. Today opens at 50.90. You measure the gap from where?
choices: Yesterday's close
Yesterday's open
Yesterday's high
Today's 30-minute high
questions.why: Yesterday's close, the red day's close. The gap is the open against yesterday's close, here 50.90 over 49.80. That's what tells you buyers paid up overnight. The red high, 51.50, has a different job. It's your trigger, not where the gap starts. This one opened under it, so you wait for price to trade through.
questions.lesson_line: The gap is measured from the red close. The red high is the trigger.

wrong.Yesterday's open: One old candle book compares opens. We measure from the close.
wrong.Yesterday's high: The red high is your trigger, not where the gap starts.
wrong.Today's 30-minute high: That's the line for the opening-range entry. The gap is the open against yesterday's close.

questions.simple: From the red day's close, because the gap is how far buyers paid up overnight.

deeper.counter: Bigalow's page says the second candle opens at the previous day's open, or gaps open. He compares opens. We measure from the red day's close, and we want a real gap there, not a flat open.

reasons: rests on our criteria card (proposed 1.5% gap) and differs from Bigalow's version

The tighter the honest stop, the more shares the same risk buys. MS in 1997 was this exact trade, and it hit 3R in two days.
questions.lesson_line: Divide by your fill. Over 3.5%, it isn't a clean Kicker.
questions.simple: It's 1.8% under your fill, well inside the 3.5% a Kicker allows.

questions.q: Account 100,000, risking 0.5% a trade. Fill 21.44, stop 20.70. Your position cap isn't in play. How many shares?

Hold, the stop isn't hit
Add on a break of the range

questions.answer: Sell it and free the money
questions.why: Sell it. Ten trading days in and it's sitting at +0.6R. A trade still under 1R after 10 days gets sold. A Kicker is supposed to kick. This one's tying up money and attention you could put on a stock that's actually moving. Don't add, and don't widen the stop. Free the money and go find the next one.

questions.q: The trade's working. Do you add on this push?
choices: Rarely, on feel, never as the plan
Yes, adding on pushes is the plan
Never, we don't add to winners
No, sell it all while it is strong
questions.story: The Kicker works. Two days later it pushes over the Kicker day's high on strong volume.
questions.answer: Rarely, on feel, never as the plan
questions.why: Rarely, and it's a feel call. The plan was the full size at one price with one stop, and that part's done. An add to a working winner on strength does happen, but you never plan it. Add on every push and you keep buying higher, so a normal pullback hits a bigger position. A push is also where you start thinking about selling some. Later sells go into strength, and the rest rides the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Full size at one price. An add on strength is rare, never the plan.

wrong.No, sell it all while it is strong: Sell some into strength if you like. Selling it all cuts the winner short.
wrong.Never, we don't add to winners: Not never. An add to a working winner on strength happens. It's just rare, and a feel call.
wrong.Yes, adding on pushes is the plan: That makes adding the routine. It's rare, and every add buys higher than your first price.

questions.simple: Rarely. An add to a working winner on strength happens, but it's a feel call, never the plan.

reasons: rests on the owner's buy-once rule (A5)

questions.q: You've been stopped out of the same Kicker stock twice this week. If it triggers again Thursday, a third try is allowed.

questions.lesson_line: After a stop-out, the next try needs a new trigger. And the tries are capped.
questions.simple: True. You get three tries a week on one stock, each on a new trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E56 and B21)

The 50-day
The 200-day
The 5-day

wrong.The 200-day: That's the line we don't buy under, not a trail.

If it opens over the red high, your market buy fills right at the open. Then your stop starts 3.5% under the fill until the first 30-minute low shows up. Entries are market orders, so a limit order isn't the answer either.

The gap comes from the numbers, not from trapped sellers. We grade it as a PEG, a Power Earnings Gap. LUV did this on 2026-01-29: a 6.2% gap and up 18.7% on 3.8x volume.

Yes, it closed up 8.4%
No, the red day closed too low
Yes, it traded through the red high

questions.why: No, there's barely a gap. It opened just 0.8% over the red close. That's close to a flat open. The Kicker's whole trick is the overnight jump that traps yesterday's sellers. Without a real gap nobody's trapped. Look where it sits on the chart too. CEG had pulled back well off its high and closed just under its 50-day. So the next day is a strong bounce, not a Kicker. It closed up 8.4%. Nice day. Different setup.

questions.q: It's fading off 49.70. Is there a trade?

Yes, the 1.7% gap is the trigger
No, a 1.7% gap is too small
Yes, buy the 49.70 high on the fade

Wait and pick the stop after the fill
Set an alert and size it by feel
Plan the entry and size at the open

questions.q: You're filled at 60.01. Where does your stop go?

choices: A few cents under the 58.40 low
Exactly on the 58.40 low so far
3.5% under the 60.01 fill price
The final low, picked at the close
questions.answer: A few cents under the 58.40 low
questions.why: A few cents under 58.40. That's the low of the day so far, and it's what you know at the fill. 3.5% under 60.01 would sit lower, so the low is the closer stop. It wins. Put it in with your broker right away. Don't wait for the day's final low. That's setting a stop after the fact, on information you didn't have.

wrong.Exactly on the 58.40 low so far: Right on the low gets tagged by the first wiggle. Go a few cents under.
wrong.3.5% under the 60.01 fill price: That's the cap. The low so far is closer, so it's your stop.
wrong.The final low, picked at the close: Too late. The stop goes in with the broker when you buy.

deeper.trap: Picking the stop from the day's final low. You can't know it when you buy, and the stop has to be a real order with the broker. Use the low so far, 58.40, and set the stop a few cents under it.

questions.q: What do you do with the stop?
questions.story: You bought a Kicker at 75.00. The broker stop sits at 73.20. At 1:00 pm the stock is at 73.60 and you feel it will bounce.
choices: Leave the order where it is
Lower it to 72.40 to give it room
Cancel it and watch the screen
Add a half position at 73.60
questions.answer: Leave the order where it is
questions.why: Leave it. 73.60 is still above your 73.20 stop, so nothing has failed yet. A stop only moves up, never down. Lower it to 72.40 and your planned loss just got bigger, because of a feeling. If it bounces, great. If it doesn't, the stop does its job at the loss you signed up for.
questions.lesson_line: A stop only moves up. If you want to lower it, the answer is no.

wrong.Cancel it and watch the screen: A stop in your head isn't a stop. The order stays with the broker.
wrong.Lower it to 72.40 to give it room: That makes your planned loss bigger. A stop never moves down.
wrong.Add a half position at 73.60: That's adding to a loser, right above your stop. Never.

questions.simple: Leave it. A stop only moves up, and a hunch isn't a reason to risk more.

deeper.trap: A hunch that it'll bounce. The one exception to a stop that only moves up is the gap rule. When a stock gaps through the stop, the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop. A dip to 73.60, above a 73.20 stop, isn't a gap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

No, a stop never moves
Yes, breakeven at 1R is fine
Sell a third now, then breakeven

questions.q: What do you do into this run?

Hold it all until the 9 EMA breaks
Sell a small part and let it run
